blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: Self-supervised training is monitored without labels, through the loss and statistics of the learned features. We report a case where we know the encoders lost part of what they had learned, so we can check whether these signals noticed. We trained LeJEPA encoders on synthetic images with known generating factors. In nine of ten seeds, the readability of those factors fell abruptly and stayed down, nearly always along the same direction in factor space. Meanwhile the loss kept falling, and most of the eleven label-free signals we tracked kept improving and rated the declining runs better than runs that did not decline. Standard change-point detection rarely flagged the decline near its onset, and selecting checkpoints by these signals mostly chose ones after it.

blocks.en: 1 Introduction
blocks.zh: 导言

blocks.en:
Self-supervised training has no labels to check against, so it is judged
by its loss and by label-free statistics of the features. SimSiam ( Chen & He, 2021 ) uses feature standard deviation to diagnose
collapse. RankMe ( Garrido et al., 2023 ) and LiDAR ( Thilak et al., 2024a ) are used to select models, and LiDAR’s authors
suggest it could also tell when to stop training. Arputharaj et al. (2026) compare many such metrics
against downstream accuracy across trained models. None of these
statistics measures whether an encoder keeps what it has already learned.
Nor can that be checked on natural data, because nobody knows what an
encoder should encode at each checkpoint.

blocks.en:
An image generator with known factors removes that problem: the
readability of each factor can be measured from frozen features at every
checkpoint. On one such generator, we trained encoders with a reduced
two-view LeJEPA ( Balestriero & LeCun, 2025 ) recipe and saw them learn the factors
and then abruptly lose part of that readability (Figure 1 ). Over
the same epochs the training loss kept falling and RankMe, a measure of
effective rank, rose. Falling effective rank is the sign of dimensional
collapse ( Jing et al., 2022 ; Garrido et al., 2023 ) , so this decline did
not look like a collapse,
and a check for collapse would have read it as progress. The two training views share the factors, so
the objective never asked the encoder to discard them. The decline
recurred across seeds and held up under nonlinear probes and a separately
generated test split. A masked autoencoder ( He et al., 2022 , MAE;) trained on the same images for the
same number of epochs did not decline.

Since we know when the encoder lost readability, we can check whether
label-free signals noticed. We tracked eleven of them around each decline
and compared the runs that declined with runs of the same settings that
did not. Most kept improving through the decline and rated the runs that
declined better than those that did not (Section 3 ). Even the
best pairing of signal and change-point method, chosen after the fact,
alarmed near the onset in only about a third of the declines; most pairings
alarmed in far fewer.
Choosing checkpoints by these signals mostly picked ones after the
decline, with worse readability. A LiDAR variant we computed by mistake
flagged most declines, but it relies on information a real training run does
not have, so it cannot serve as a monitor (Section 5 ).

blocks.en: 2 Experimental Setup and Measurements

blocks.en:
We use a simpler configuration of the
simulator of Kakati (2026) , built on PyCaloFlash v1.0 ( Dreyer et al., 2026 ) , to generate sparse images from two shape
coordinates, ( z 1 , z 2 ) (z_{1},z_{2}) , and energy E E . Each image has 4 channels of 64 × 64 64\times 64 pixels and shows one pattern at a fixed
position. The shape coordinates set how the pattern’s intensity is spread
over the channels: where it peaks and how broad the peak is. E E sets the
overall intensity and shifts the typical peak position and width
(Appendix A ). In each channel, N N points, called
elements, are drawn at random from this intensity profile and binned into
the pixels. The element count controls image graininess (Figure 5 ). Each image’s shape
coordinates are drawn from a distribution set by a parameter μ \mu . At μ = 0 \mu=0 each coordinate is standard normal; as μ \mu grows, its distribution
splits into two Gaussians whose centres move apart at fixed overall variance,
and near μ = 1 \mu=1 they barely overlap.
Instead of image augmentations, the
two training views are independent renders with the same shape and energy;
only the sampled elements differ.
Figure 1 a shows a training pair and the two measurement
paths, and Appendix A describes the generator’s physical
model.

condition. Effective rank is measured with RankMe ( Garrido et al., 2023 ) , the exponential of the entropy of the normalized
singular values of the same features. Appendix B gives the

blocks.en: 4 Checking and Understanding the Decline
blocks.zh: 4 检查和了解下降

blocks.en:
We first check that the decline does not depend on the readout and that the
rise in effective rank does not depend on how it is measured
(Section 4.1 ), then show that nearly all declines share

blocks.en: 5 LiDAR Flags the Decline When Its Groups Redraw Shape

blocks.en:
LiDAR measures how evenly the differences between groups of inputs
spread across feature directions, after discounting the variation
inside each group. Normally, each group holds views made the same way as
the training views. By mistake, our first evaluation built its groups with an
augmentation from the paper that introduced the simulator ( Kakati, 2026 , §2) :
every render in a group keeps the group’s energy but
gets a newly drawn shape, whereas training views share both. With groups
that redraw shape, LiDAR flagged most declines on time, with few false
alarms; with training-view groups, it rarely did
(Figure 6 ). With shape redrawn inside each
group, the groups differ mainly in energy, so the largest direction in
LiDAR’s spectrum follows energy. As the decline lowers
energy readability, that direction weakens, the spectrum evens out, and
LiDAR rises (Appendix G ).

blocks.en: 6 Related Work
blocks.zh: 6 相关工作

blocks.en:
The label-free signals we track were mostly validated by comparing models.
RankMe ( Garrido et al., 2023 ) and LiDAR ( Thilak et al., 2024a ) were
tested on trained models and sets of checkpoints, and LeJEPA’s training
loss correlated with downstream linear-probe accuracy over training
configurations ( Balestriero & LeCun, 2025 ) . Within a single run of I-JEPA ( Assran et al., 2023 ) , Thilak et al. (2024a) also found that effective rank peaked early and then
fell, with the best downstream accuracy far from that peak. The closest
work to ours, Arputharaj et al. (2026) , compares label-free metrics
with downstream accuracy for many trained models and finds that each
metric’s reliability depends on architecture and training objective. We
ask a different question, whether these signals notice when a single run
loses what it learned, so our result does not contradict theirs. Online
linear probes, as in solo-learn ( Turrisi da Costa et al., 2022 ) , follow what
the features encode during training, but they need labels, as do the
probes that measure the decline here.

Effective rank measures how evenly the features spread over directions,
not what they encode, so it can rise while readability falls. RankMe

largest direction of the features’ spectrum; its share fell, which made

possible cause is feature suppression, where easy features hold back the

channel, also found it harder to read than most directions. So the common

hardest direction for both puts little weight on energy, so neither

blocks.en: 8 Limitations
blocks.zh: 8 限制

blocks.en:
The evidence comes from one image generator, small encoders and a reduced
two-view LeJEPA recipe, and MAE is the only other objective that learned
on it. It does
not show how common the decline is on natural images or with the
published eight-view recipe at scale ( Balestriero & LeCun, 2025 ) . A contrastive
model trained with SimCLR’s loss ( Chen et al., 2020 ) never moved away
from its initialization on this generator, and changing the learning rate
did not help, so we do not know whether contrastive training shows the
decline. Readability is what our probes recover, so the decline shows that
the factors became harder to read; it does not show that the information
is gone. We also tested only three
standard change-point detection methods, with thresholds set on control runs from
another shape distribution. That they rarely alarmed in time does not
show that the decline cannot be detected from these signals.

blocks.en: 9 Conclusion
blocks.zh: 9 结论

blocks.en:
In this LeJEPA case study, the encoders lost readability they had
learned, while the training loss kept falling and most label-free signals
kept improving. Change-point detection on these signals caught a third of the declines in
time at best, and checkpoints chosen by loss or RankMe came
at or after the onset, with worse readability than earlier ones. A signal
that keeps improving therefore does not show that an encoder keeps what it
has learned.

blocks.en:
We use a single-particle configuration of the simulator of Kakati (2026, §2 and App. A) , whose images show several
overlapping particles. The simulator uses
PyCaloFlash v1.0 ( Dreyer et al., 2026 ) , a simplified model of a particle shower in a calorimeter, a layered detector
that absorbs a high-energy particle and records where its energy is
deposited. Each of the 4 channels of the 64 × 64 64\times 64 image is one detector layer, at increasing
depth, and each pixel holds the energy deposited in one cell of that layer.
Each layer samples N N elements (individual deposits) independently from a smooth intensity
profile, and the two views of a training pair share the profile and differ
only in these samples. Energies are in MeV (megaelectronvolts). Raw cell
values x x are transformed as log ⁡ ( 1 + x ) / log ⁡ ( 1 + 5500 ) \log(1+x)/\log(1+5500) .

(5.40M parameters). We used AdamW ( Loshchilov & Hutter, 2019 ) with batch

blocks.en:
We audited the training
loss, SIGReg, feature standard deviation, LiDAR, the 21
variants of the seven metrics, RankMe and LiDAR on the projector output,
and LiDAR with groups that redraw shape (Section 5 ). On each series we ran three standard
change-point detection methods, CUSUM, EWMA and Page–Hinkley, with
thresholds set on separate control runs at μ = 0.97 \mu=0.97 . Alarms were
scored on 41 runs: the ten default runs, the wide-projector runs at otherwise
default settings (ten trained for 300 epochs and three for 150), and the
first three seeds per projector at μ = 0.4 \mu=0.4 , 0.7 and 0.9. Of these, 28
declined and the other 13 did not. Before any fitting,
wide-projector series are cut at epoch 150 and default-projector series at 300. Two

epochs of their onsets extends past the cut; the matched analyses use the
other 26 decline runs. Each projector has four control runs at μ = 0.97 \mu=0.97 . Thresholds came from two procedures: an initial one that
standardizes each run against its own early epochs, and a
control-referenced check that compares each run with the controls’ median
change at the same epoch. We designed the second after seeing the first’s
results, and neither has a nominal false-alarm guarantee.
